title: Edmonton police officer saves stabbed man's life
article: Police are hunting for a culprit after a 26-year-old man was stabbed in the chest inside a NAIT-area Boston Pizza lounge Thursday night.
Currently hospitalized in serious condition, police say the man's life was saved by a female constable who was first on scene.
The violence broke out around 9:30 p.m. inside the Boston Pizza at 118 Avenue and 101 Street when an argument escalated to bloodshed.
The victim was stabbed before the assailant fled the lounge.
The constable patrolling in the area was the first to arrive at the scene after the 911 call. She found the victim bleeding profusely.
"He was really badly injured. He had a stab wound in the upper torso of his body," said police spokeswoman Patrycia Thenu.
The officer provided emergency care, placing pressure on the wound until paramedics arrived.
"Police were told by medical staff at the hospital that if it hadn't been for her actions, the complainant most likely wouldn't have survived."
A search by North Division cops and the canine unit - with an Air 1 helicopter searching from the sky - turned up empty.
The assailant escaped but the two men were known to each other, said cops who are actively working to arrest him.
The attack happened so fast that staff barely had time to react to the stabbing, said Jeff Loewen, general manager of the NAIT Boston Pizza.
"It had to have been a targeted hit because he was in here for less than 30 seconds," said Loewen.
"Nobody really knew what was happening until they started seeing the blood trail."

Loewen said the suspect stepped out of a cab, walked into the lounge and directly over the pool tables, where the victim was having a drink. In a matter of seconds, the man "did his deed" before sprinting through the front doors.
Staff immediately dialed 911 and continued to assist the officer when she arrived minutes later.
"She kinda took over and let the staff back away and yeah, she saved his life," said Loewen, adding that some staff were "shaken up" by the violence.
The officer's supervisors have recommended or will be recommending her for a commendation, said Thenu, but police can not name the hero cop due to "officer safety issues."
Since 2009, every recruit and patrol officer has been required to take a casualty care course to provide life-saving aid while waiting for paramedics.
The course was started by Const. Jason Mitchell after Darren James Cardinal, 27, was killed when he opened fire on Const. Dan Furman on June 30, 2006 in a basement duplex.
Had Mitchell not had previous medical training from the army, Furman - who was critically injured when Cardinal shot him - likely would have died from his injuries.
